title: Utah Legal Regulatory Sandbox — Phase 2 policy changes (Utah Supreme Court letter to the Legal Services Innovation Committee, 5 September 2024, and Innovation Office Phase 2 page)
pub: Utah Supreme Court / Office of Legal Services Innovation
author: Utah Supreme Court · Utah Office of Legal Services Innovation

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, context-specific deployment and materially extends the cluster with a regulatory operating model: concentrate limited oversight on higher-potential service models, use front-end consumer protections, and tailor evidence collection through pre- and post-launch audits. It does not establish AI task capability or verification findings, but provides a concrete institutional example of risk-based governance and access-to-justice-focused redesign.
qs: Last year, the Court made several changes to the Sandbox to promote our objective of increasing access to legal services without increasing the risk of consumer harm.

Similarly, any changes to the way we collect and analyze data will be informed by the type of entities being regulated, recognizing that the most useful data concerning mid- to high-level entities will come from pre- and post-launch audits.

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between merely opening ownership and achieving meaningful access to justice. Utah’s Phase 2 narrows participation toward models expected to reach underserved Utah consumers, citing regulatory burdens and limited consumer benefit from many low-innovation, ABS-only entities. It presents improved access as a goal and predicted benefit, not a demonstrated outcome.
qs: Based on the information gathered so far, the Court has decided to narrow the scope of the Sandbox to models that demonstrate the most potential to narrow the access to justice gap in Utah by reaching underserved Utahns.

A number of low-innovation entities have consumed a disproportionate amount of Innovation Office resources that could be better spent processing applications and regulating entities with more potential to benefit consumers.

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: The source directly endorses the cluster’s central framing of the Sandbox as a conditional experiment testing access gains against consumer harm, rather than as unrestricted deregulation or proof of success. Its Phase 2 changes further support the synthesis by tying authorization to innovative services for underserved Utah consumers and improving the focus of oversight and evidence collection.
qs: Office of Legal Services Innovation — Phase 2 page (captured 2026-08-16)  Sandbox Phase 2 – Utah Office of Legal Services Innovation  **  Phase 2 of the Utah Legal Regulatory Sandbox**  The Utah Supreme Court’s legal regulatory Sandbox is a seven-year pilot project designed to test whether changing the way it regulates the practice of law can narrow the access-to-justice gap without increasing consumer harm.
To meet the innovation requirement, an entity must demonstrate that a              Sandbox authorization will allow it to reach Utah consumers currently              underserved by the legal market.

mo.t: Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier

kp.k: Sandbox tests access gains without increased consumer harm
kp.d: The Innovation Office describes a seven-year regulatory pilot. The Court’s September 5, 2024 letter retains the existing Sandbox model while narrowing its scope to improve testing and inform future regulation. The document concerns legal-service innovation and regulatory structures, rather than reporting AI-specific performance or outcomes.
qs: The Utah Supreme Court’s legal regulatory Sandbox is a seven-year pilot project designed to test whether changing the way it regulates the practice of law can narrow the access-to-justice gap without increasing consumer harm.
The results of this experiment will inform the Court’s future decisions governing the practice of law in Utah.
Based on your feedback, we have decided to continue with the existing Sandbox model.

kp.k: Participation now requires substantial relevance to underserved Utah consumers
kp.d: The Court modifies the innovation requirement to include a Utah nexus and a high threshold for participation. Applicants must demonstrate that authorization enables an innovative model to reach underserved Utah consumers. Utah impact must be substantial relative to the entity’s overall reach: incidental Utah business by national or international companies does not qualify, whereas principally Utah-focused small entities may qualify despite modest client numbers.
qs: The innovation requirement will be modified to include a Utah nexus.
National and international companies that expect to serve
only an incidental number of Utah clients will not qualify.
A small entity
that principally serves Utah consumers will satisfy the Utah nexus even if
it reaches a modest number of clients.

kp.k: Existing authorizations lose their previous innovation exemption
kp.d: Previously authorized entities with satisfactory compliance records had been allowed to remain regardless of the innovation requirement. Phase 2 instead requires assessment of each existing entity’s authorized service model and exit for those not meeting the Utah innovation requirement. Entities proposing a different model must reapply. Nonlawyer ownership alone is insufficient unless it facilitates an innovative model with substantial Utah impact; mid- to high-innovation models generally qualify when designed to reach substantial numbers of Utah consumers.
qs: However, previously authorized entities with a satisfactory compliance record were allowed to continue to operate within the Sandbox regardless of whether they met the innovation requirement.
All previously authorized entities that do not meet the Utah innovation
requirement will exit the Sandbox.
Low-innovation entities will not meet the Utah innovation
requirement unless the non-lawyer ownership structure is designed
to facilitate an innovative service model with a substantial impact on
the Utah market, such as providing a one-stop-shop or intermediary
platform for Utah consumers.

kp.k: Court identifies resource burdens and authorization misuse
kp.d: The Court reports that some low-innovation entities consumed disproportionate regulatory resources. It says some alternative business structure entities appeared to use authorization to imply Court endorsement or access restricted advertising markets, while many appeared to misunderstand authorization as permission to provide services through non-Utah-licensed attorneys. Investigating that misunderstanding revealed a sizeable group without meaningful Utah market presence. These are the Court’s reported observations, not quantified outcome findings.
qs: A number of low-innovation entities have consumed a disproportionate amount of Innovation Office resources that could be better spent processing applications and regulating entities with more potential to benefit consumers.

Some ABS entities appear to have misused their Sandbox authorization to bolster their credibility or gain access to restricted advertising markets by suggesting that their services have been endorsed by this Court.
And many ABS entities appear to have misconstrued their authorizations as permitting them to offer legal services provided by non-Utah-licensed attorneys.
While attempting to correct this misconception, we discovered that a sizeable group has no meaningful presence in the Utah legal market.

kp.k: Narrowing aims to improve evidence and regulatory capacity
kp.d: The Court reports that its data team found the number and variety of participating entities challenging for meaningful data collection and analysis. With the Sandbox approaching four years of operation at the end of September 2024, the Court expects a major reduction in participants and a shift of limited resources toward mid- and high-innovation entities. It reports that three-fourths of current participants are low-innovation, ABS-only entities. The expected resource and access benefits are policy expectations, not demonstrated results of Phase 2.
qs: Finally, we learned from our data team that the number and variety of entities in the Sandbox poses significant challenges for collecting and analyzing data in a meaningful way.
At the end of this month, the Sandbox will have been in operation for four years.
We anticipate that these two policy changes will vastly reduce the number of entities in the Sandbox.
Currently, three-fourths of the Sandbox consists of low- innovation, ABS-only entities.

kp.k: Audits remain central to consumer-harm monitoring
kp.d: The Court orders audits restarted immediately, retaining the Committee’s existing process and paid auditors because participant fees cover their costs. It endorses audits of mid- to high-innovation entities as the most valuable consumer-harm information source. Earlier safeguards included additional vetting, pre-launch audits for high-innovation entities, and core fiduciary duties for financing and controlling persons. Future complaint classification and data changes are deferred until the population is narrowed.
qs: Restart the audit process immediately.
We agree that the audit process developed by
the Committee has been successful and should not be modified.

To mitigate consumer harm, we introduced a series of front-end controls: additional vetting of participants, pre-launch audits for high-innovation entities, and the requirement that financing and controlling persons adhere to the same core fiduciary duties that lawyers owe to their clients.
A rubric for classifying and handling complaints will be more helpful if it is tailored to the more limited variety of entities that will remain in the Sandbox.

kp.k: Badge removal addresses misleading impressions of Court endorsement
kp.d: The Court adopts the Committee’s recommendation to retire the Sandbox badge because of concerns about misuse or misconstrual as an endorsement. Participating entities must instead prominently solicit complaints or feedback, with the stated aim of obtaining information about consumer benefits as well as harms.
qs: Retire the badge and in its place require entities to prominently display
language to solicit complaints or feedback.
misused or misconstrued as an endorsement by the Court.
This recommendation
also furthers the Court’s interest in soliciting not just complaints, but feedback on
benefits to consumers.

kp.k: Prospective for-profit immigration providers face exclusion
kp.d: The Court adopts the Committee’s recommendation to reject applicants solely or primarily offering for-profit immigration-related services, agreeing that these models offer little consumer-friendly innovation and disproportionate consumer-harm risk. The supplied document references a Committee memorandum but does not reproduce its supporting evidence. Other pending and new applications are to continue so that additional service models can inform policy.
qs: Reject applications from for-profit entities solely or primarily offering
immigration-related services.
entities offer little potential for consumer-friendly innovations and pose an
outsized risk of consumer harm.
Continue processing applications for new Sandbox entities.

kp.k: Exit arrangements distinguish unnecessary authorization from disciplinary exposure
kp.d: The Court specifies three potential dispositions: termination, termination with accommodation, or provisional status. It suggests some entities need no authorization, including some legal-information or scrivener providers and some nonlawyer-owned arrangements that do not require fee-sharing or IOLTA accommodations. For lawyers in some ABS-only entities, the Court offers possible protection from discipline for existing authorized arrangements, restricted to the current structure or model and non-transferable to other Utah attorneys. Provisional status may apply to qualifying authorized models not yet launched.
qs: Terminate Sandbox Authorization.
Entities that offer
only legal information or scrivener services are likely not engaged in
the practice of law and do not need special authorization to operate
in Utah, especially if they operate using the same model in other
states.
Terminate Sandbox Authorization with Accommodation.
That exemption will be non-transferable to other Utah attorneys and
limited to the existing ownership structure and/or business model.
Change Authorization to Provisional Status.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit claim about AI. Its claims concern regulatory experimentation and innovative legal-service models: the Utah Supreme Court predicts that narrowing Sandbox participation will concentrate resources on models with greater potential to address unmet legal need in Utah.
pts.d: The Court frames increased access without increased consumer harm as the hypothesis being tested, not an established outcome. It predicts a substantial reduction in Sandbox entities and more focused regulation of mid- and high-innovation models. It also reports that some low-innovation entities disproportionately consume regulatory resources, that some ABS entities appear to misuse authorization as implied Court endorsement, and that many appear to misunderstand its licensing implications. Separately, it judges prospective for-profit providers primarily offering immigration services to have little consumer-friendly innovation potential and outsized consumer-harm risk. Neither the letter nor the Office's page identifies innovation levels with AI use, so these claims should not be presented as findings about AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The Court relies on Sandbox operating experience, Committee feedback, a Committee memorandum, and data-team observations; the document does not supply measured access improvements or consumer-harm rates.
pts.d: The September 2024 letter reports that three-fourths of participating entities are low-innovation, ABS-only entities. It describes resource burdens, apparent authorization misuse, and discovery that a sizeable group lacks a meaningful Utah market presence. The Court attributes concerns about meaningful data collection and analysis to its data team and the immigration-provider recommendation to a Committee memorandum whose supporting analysis is not reproduced. It calls audits the most valuable source of consumer-harm information, but provides no audit results or AI-specific evidence. Expected benefits from narrowing participation remain policy predictions rather than demonstrated effects in this document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The predictions accompany the September 5, 2024 Phase 2 changes, near the Sandbox's fourth anniversary; benefits depend on implementing a substantive Utah-focused innovation requirement.
pts.d: The Office's page describes a seven-year pilot. The letter gives no date by which access improvements will occur. New applicants must demonstrate potential to reach underserved Utah consumers, and existing entities must undergo individualized review of their authorized models. Utah impact must be substantial relative to overall reach: incidental Utah business by national or international companies is insufficient, whereas a small principally Utah-serving entity can satisfy the geographic nexus with modest client numbers. Low-innovation ownership arrangements qualify only when designed to facilitate an innovative model with substantial Utah impact. Qualifying but unlaunched models may receive provisional status rather than outright removal.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are underserved Utah consumers; the immediate effects concern Sandbox providers, their lawyers, prospective immigration-service entrants, and regulatory staff.
pts.d: The Court expects to redirect regulatory capacity toward models with greater access-to-justice potential. Existing entities failing the requirement will leave the Sandbox, although the Court says some need no special authorization to continue operating. Some lawyers in ABS-only entities may receive non-transferable accommodations limited to existing ownership structures or business models, protecting continuation of authorized arrangements from professional discipline. Prospective for-profit entities solely or primarily offering immigration-related services will no longer be authorized. Consumers will be invited to submit complaints or benefits-related feedback through prominent language replacing the Sandbox badge. No specific effects on AI vendors, AI-enabled providers, legal employment, or legal-service prices are stated.
